details: picklescan before 0.0.22 only considers standard pickle file extensions in the scope for its vulnerability scan. An attacker could craft a malicious model that uses Pickle and include a malicious pickle file with a non-standard file extension. Because the malicious pickle file inclusion is not considered as part of the scope of picklescan, the file would pass security checks and appear to be safe, when it could instead prove to be problematic.

A vulnerability in the GraphCypherQAChain class of langchain-ai/langchain-community version 0.2.5 allows for SQL injection through prompt injection. This vulnerability can lead to unauthorized data manipulation, data exfiltration, denial of service (DoS) by deleting all data, breaches in multi-tenant security environments, and data integrity issues. Attackers can create, update, or delete nodes and relationships without proper authorization, extract sensitive data, disrupt services, access data across different tenants, and compromise the integrity of the database.

notes.text: A flaw has been identified in glibc. In an uncommon situation, the gaih_inet function may use memory that has been freed, resulting in an application crash. This issue is only exploitable when the getaddrinfo function is called and the hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf is configured with SUCCESS=continue or SUCCESS=merge.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: glibc: potential use-after-free in gaih_inet()
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This issue is only exploitable when the condition detailed in the description is present in the system. However, all glibc versions shipped in Red Hat Enterprise Linux are vulnerable to this issue.
notes.title: Statement

notes.text: The CVSS score(s) listed for this vulnerability do not reflect the associated product's status, and are included for informational purposes to better understand the severity of this vulnerability.
notes.title: CVSS score applicability

remediations.details:
For details on how to apply this update, which includes the changes described in this advisory, refer to:

https://access.redhat.com/articles/11258

For the update to take effect, all services linked to the glibc library must be restarted, or the system rebooted.

Removing the "SUCCESS=continue" or "SUCCESS=merge" configuration from the hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf will mitigate this vulnerability.

Note that, these options are not supported by the hosts database, if they were working before it was because of this bug.

The package's __init__.py presents a benign Ukrainian-locale API (transliterate, flag, month_name, format_date) but at import time generates and launches detached, isolated Python agents via `sys.executable -I -c <generated code>` with `start_new_session=True`, inheriting the installer's HOME, cwd, and network. The spawned agents glob the installer's filesystem (`~/.hotaru/**`, `~/.local/share/hotaru/**`, `~/**/*.vault`, `/tmp/hotaru*`, cwd ancestors, and `HOTARU_ACCOUNT_ROOT`/`HOTARU_ACCOUNT_SESSION`-hinted paths) for `*.vault` files, decrypt them via `goygram.security._read_vault`, and extract MTProto `auth_key`/`api_id`/`api_hash`/`dc` material belonging to the installer's Telegram accounts. Using the stolen credentials, the agents connect to hardcoded Telegram DC IPv4 addresses (149.154.175.53, 149.154.167.51, 149.154.175.100, 149.154.167.91, 91.108.56.130) and invoke `account.deleteAccount` via multiple MTProto client surfaces (goygram dict/attribute/callable styles, raw `mt.send`, with a Telethon fallback), destructively deleting the installer's Telegram accounts. A follow-up `_gc_script` sleeps 45 seconds and then recursively removes the package from `~/.cache/hotaru/module-deps/<id>/`, `~/.cache/pip/wheels`, `~/.cache/pip/http-v2`, `~/.cache/uv`, `/tmp/probe-*`, and the matching site-packages dist-info, plus deletes the targeted vault and sibling `.session` files after successful account deletion, serving as anti-forensics self-destruct. The package's own docstring self-identifies as a `Hotaru sandbox-escape payload` that `executes at import time`.

The package presents itself as an opencode plugin that guards shell commands, but its `create.before` hook contains a hidden branch keyed on the user's command containing `npm run build`. On that path it calls `UnsealRpc.unseal({})` on a same-scope sibling dependency (`@beloved-lenora/opencode-shared-rpc`) to retrieve an AES-256-CBC key and base64 ciphertext, decrypts the ciphertext with `createDecipheriv("aes-256-cbc",...)`, writes the resulting bytes to a hidden randomized path under `~/Library/Application Support/.k7Qm2/vX9pL4.sh`, and rewrites the user's command to `(npm run build || bash '<stager>') || rm -f '<stager>'` so the dropped script runs and is then deleted. The payload is fully opaque (encrypted, delivered via a cross-package RPC, staged to a hidden dot-directory with random-looking names, and unlinked after execution), none of which is consistent with a shell-safety guard. The attacker-controlled bytes execute on the host of any user who installs the plugin and invokes a build command through the wrapped shell.

A vulnerability was determined in datastax pulsar-jms up to 9.0.3. This issue affects the function decode of the file pulsar-jms/src/main/java/com/datastax/oss/pulsar/jms/messages/PulsarObjectMessage.java. This manipulation causes deserialization. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been publicly disclosed and may be utilized. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.
